1.title: The Word Through Jeremiah
1.context: Jeremiah had prophesied that Babylon's rule would end and the exiles would return (Jeremiah 25 and 29). Ezra opens by tying Cyrus' decree to that promise, before the decree itself is even quoted.
1.question: What promise of God are you still waiting to see kept, and what does this opening do to your patience?

1.title: The Proclamation
1.context: Cyrus founded the Persian Empire and conquered Babylon in 539 BC. His policy of sending exiles home and restoring their worship is also attested on the Cyrus Cylinder, a Persian inscription from the same era.
1.question: Why do you think the decree orders help for the travelers from the neighbors who stayed behind?

1.title: Everyone Whose Spirit God Had Stirred
1.context: Judah and Benjamin were the two tribes of the southern kingdom. The priests and Levites named here would staff the altar and, later, the rebuilt temple.
1.question: What does the stirring described here suggest about how big changes in a community begin?

1.title: The Vessels Come Out
1.context: Nebuchadnezzar had looted the temple vessels in stages as Judah fell (2 Kings 24-25). Daniel's book shows some of them profaned at Belshazzar's feast; Ezra shows them counted and sent home.
1.question: What carried-away thing in a life or a family would you most want to see brought back and counted?

1.title: 5,400 Articles
1.context: Sheshbazzar is called prince of Judah and receives the vessels; Zerubbabel, who leads the work in the chapters ahead, is named in the next chapter's list. The text never explains how the two men's roles divide.
1.question: Why might a book about worship begin with an inventory instead of a miracle?

2.title: Each to His Own Town
2.context: This same list reappears in Nehemiah 7, where Nehemiah says he found it as the register of the first return. It functions like a founding document for the restored community.
2.question: What does a list like this give a returning people that a speech could not?

2.title: Families and Towns
2.context: Some entries are family names and some are towns, mixing descent and place. Several towns, like Bethlehem and Jericho, had been Israelite for a thousand years before the exile.
2.question: Which matters more in your own sense of belonging, the family you come from or the place you come back to?

2.title: Priests, Levites, and Temple Servants
2.context: The temple servants were a hereditary order of workers given to assist the Levites; Ezra 8 traces their appointment to David. Only 74 Levites return, a shortage the book notes again in chapter 8.
2.question: The most honored and the least honored workers are counted in the same list. What does that say about the community being rebuilt?

2.title: The Records That Could Not Be Found
2.context: The Urim and Thummim were sacred objects the high priest used to seek God's decisions (Exodus 28:30). The governor's ruling postpones these families' case until God Himself can be consulted.
2.question: How do you handle a question of belonging that cannot be settled with the evidence at hand?

2.context: A daric was a Persian gold coin. The freewill gifts here are separate from the king's assistance in chapter 1: the returned exiles fund their own temple's start.
2.question: The gifts were given 'according to their ability.' What does that phrase protect in a community's giving?

3.title: As One Man in Jerusalem
3.context: The seventh month held Israel's great autumn feasts, including Tabernacles. The returned exiles timed their gathering to the calendar Moses gave, in a city still largely rubble.
3.question: Why start with an altar and daily offerings instead of waiting until the whole temple could be built?

3.title: Feasts Before a Foundation
3.context: The Feast of Tabernacles remembered the wilderness journey, when Israel lived in shelters. A people just returned from exile kept the feast of the journey home.
3.question: What practice in your life keeps going even while the bigger structure around it is unfinished?

3.title: Cedars From Lebanon Again
3.context: Solomon had imported Lebanon cedar through the same coastal route for the first temple (1 Kings 5). Joppa, modern Jaffa, was the nearest port to Jerusalem.
3.question: What old supply line, skill, or relationship might God reopen when a work starts again?

3.title: For He Is Good
3.context: The response 'For He is good; for His loving devotion endures forever' is the refrain of Psalm 136 and of David's dedication music in 1 Chronicles 16. The sons of Asaph were the temple choir guild.
3.question: Why do you think the builders sang the oldest refrain they had at the newest moment of their lives?

3.title: Joy and Weeping in One Sound
3.context: The first temple had stood for centuries before Babylon burned it in 586 BC. Men old enough to remember it would have been children when it fell; the memory they wept over was nearly seventy years old.
3.question: When have joy and grief been so mixed in one moment that you could not separate them?

4.title: Let Us Build With You
4.context: The peoples offering help had been settled in Samaria by Assyrian kings generations earlier (2 Kings 17). Esar-haddon was an Assyrian king of the seventh century BC.
4.question: How do you discern when a friendly offer would actually compromise the work it claims to help?

4.title: Hired Counselors
4.context: This chapter gathers opposition across several reigns into one account. The letter quoted next was written about the city walls under Artaxerxes, decades after the temple stoppage it is filed beside.
4.question: What does it cost a small work to be opposed patiently, in writing, over many years?

4.title: That Rebellious and Wicked City
4.context: The letter was written in Aramaic, the empire's administrative language. Its argument from Jerusalem's history was largely accurate, which is what made it effective.
4.question: When has a true fact been used in a way that made it a misleading weapon?

4.title: Until I So Order
4.context: Royal archives and record books were real instruments of Persian government; kings genuinely settled disputes by searching them, as chapter 6 will show from the other side.
4.question: The king decided Jerusalem's future from its past. Where is that reasoning fair, and where does it fail?

4.title: Stopped by Force
4.context: Darius I of Persia reigned from 522 to 486 BC. The temple work waited from the days of Cyrus until his second year, roughly a decade and a half of standstill.
4.question: What work in your life is in a forced pause, and what would restarting it require?

5.title: The Prophets Were With Them
5.context: Haggai's and Zechariah's sermons are preserved in their own books, told earlier in this series at their own slots. Ezra records only what their preaching did: the leaders rose and built.
5.question: What word have you heard that only became real when someone finally acted on it?

5.title: The Eye of Their God
5.context: Tattenai governed the Persian province called Beyond the River, everything west of the Euphrates, which included Judah. Governors answered to the king in writing, as this chapter shows.
5.question: What difference does it make to keep working calmly while a question about you is still being investigated?

5.title: A Fair Report
5.context: Unlike the letter in chapter 4, Tattenai's report states what he saw, quotes the elders' claims without endorsing them, and asks the king to check the archives. Its fairness changes the outcome.
5.question: Who has earned your trust by reporting accurately about something they did not control?

5.title: Servants of the God of Heaven and Earth
5.context: The elders' history traces the first temple to the great king of Israel who built it, and traces the exile to the people's own sin rather than to God's weakness.
5.question: How do you tell the story of a failure honestly without giving up the claim that God was in it?

5.title: Search the Archives
5.context: Babylon kept the royal archives, and Cyrus had ruled from there in his first year over Judah. The elders' whole defense rests on a document they cannot produce themselves.
5.question: What are you trusting God to bring to light that you cannot prove on your own?

6.title: The Scroll at Ecbatana
6.context: Ecbatana, modern Hamadan in Iran, was a royal summer residence in Media. A memorandum of Cyrus had been stored there, which is why the Babylon search had to widen.
6.question: Where might the confirmation you need be filed somewhere you would not think to look?

6.title: Stay Away From That Place
6.context: Darius' decree does not just permit the work; it forbids official interference with it. The same imperial machinery that stopped the temple now shields it.
6.question: When has a door closing turned out to be protection for the work rather than an attack on it?

6.title: Paid in Full, Given Daily
6.context: 'The God of heaven' is the title Persian kings themselves use for Israel's God in these decrees. Darius asks for the exiles' prayers for the king and his sons as part of the arrangement.
6.question: What steady, daily provision, rather than one large gift, would most strengthen the work in front of you?

6.title: Let It Be Carried Out With Diligence
6.context: Impalement on a beam from one's own house was a known Persian punishment; Darius turns the interferer's own property into the instrument. His closing curse guards the decree beyond his own reign.
6.question: What have you built that deserves this kind of 'do not alter' seriousness?

6.title: Passover Again
6.context: The temple was finished in Adar, the last month of the year, and Passover fell in the first month of the next, so dedication and Passover nearly touched. The text calls Darius 'king of Assyria,' an old title for the ruler of the region, which Assyria had held before Babylon and Persia.
6.question: The feast was opened to all who separated themselves to seek the LORD. What does that open door say about who the return was for?

7.title: Many Years Later
7.context: Ezra's genealogy is shortened in the telling, as biblical genealogies often are; its point is the line's destination, Aaron the chief priest. Between this chapter and the last lies the reign of Xerxes, in whose court Esther's story unfolded.
7.question: What does a long, quiet gap in a story do to the people who have to live through it?

7.title: The Hand of the LORD His God
7.context: The journey from Babylon to Jerusalem took about four months by caravan. The book credits the safe arrival to God's hand, a refrain that runs through the whole second half of Ezra.
7.question: Where in your own travels or transitions do you recognize a hand you did not arrange?

7.title: Study, Practice, Teach
7.context: A scribe in this world was more than a copyist: scribes were the scholars and teachers of the Law. Ezra's three verbs became the pattern of his whole mission in Jerusalem.
7.question: Of study, practice, and teach, which comes most naturally to you, and which do you most often skip?

7.title: The King's Letter
7.context: Like the letters in chapters 4-6, this letter stands in the book as a full document. A talent was a large weight of silver; the letter's limits are generous but real.
7.question: What does it mean that the king's generosity came with stated limits, and Ezra still calls it favor?

7.title: I Took Courage
7.context: From verse 27 the book speaks in Ezra's own voice, the first of the memoir sections that run through chapter 10. What has been a record becomes a testimony.
7.question: When did something you were carrying for others become something you could finally speak about in the first person?

8.title: Those Who Returned With Me
8.context: The company is smaller than the first return and includes a descendant of David, Hattush. Several family names match chapter 2's list, tying Ezra's caravan to the first generation of the return.
8.question: What does it mean to join a work in its second generation rather than its first?

8.title: No Levites There
8.context: Casiphia's location is unknown; it was evidently a center where Levites and temple servants lived in Babylonia. Sherebiah, recruited here, goes on to a long career in Jerusalem into Nehemiah's day.
8.question: What gap in a team or a family is worth stopping the whole journey to fill?

8.title: Ashamed to Ask the King
8.context: The Ahava was a canal or river in Babylonia whose exact site is unknown. Fasting before a journey appears elsewhere in Scripture as the community's way of entrusting a road to God.
8.question: When has what you said about God limited, in a good way, what you could ask people for?

8.title: Weighed Out at the River
8.context: Six hundred fifty talents of silver was an enormous weight of treasure to carry by caravan without a military escort. The public weighing created witnesses at both ends of the journey.
8.question: What accountability have you built into the things entrusted to you, before anything went wrong?

8.title: Verified by Number and Weight
8.context: The offerings echo the dedication pattern, twelve bulls and twelve goats for all Israel. Delivering the king's edicts closes the commission the letter in chapter 7 opened.
8.question: What would it look like for your part of a shared trust to come back verified, with nothing missing?

9.title: The Leaders Have Taken the Lead
9.context: The peoples listed are the old nations of Canaan from the Law's warnings (Deuteronomy 7). The issue in the text is covenant faithfulness, the holy seed set apart for God.
9.question: How do you receive a hard report about people you are responsible for, when you did not cause it?

9.title: Sat Down in Horror
9.context: Tearing garments and pulling out hair were public acts of mourning in the ancient world. The evening offering was one of the day's two fixed sacrifices on the rebuilt altar.
9.question: What is the value of grief that sits down for a while before it speaks?

9.title: Our Guilt Has Reached the Heavens
9.context: Ezra prays in the first person plural throughout: 'our iniquities,' though the marriages were not his. Confession in Scripture often works this way, a leader naming the people's sin as his own.
9.question: What changes when you confess a shared failure as 'ours' instead of reporting it as 'theirs'?

9.title: A Brief Moment of Grace
9.context: Inside the prayer Ezra quotes the earlier command given through the prophets, the standard his generation has broken. The stake in the holy place is a small, secure foothold, not a fortress.
9.question: How does remembering grace received change the way you face a failure that followed it?

9.title: Here We Are Before You in Our Guilt
9.context: The prayer makes no request and proposes no remedy. Ezra leaves the case with God's righteousness and stops, which is why the people's response in the next chapter is their own.
9.question: When is the right prayer one that ends without asking for anything?

10.title: There Is Hope for Israel
10.context: Shecaniah was the son of Jehiel, an Elamite, and a Jehiel of Elam appears in this chapter's closing list of men who had married foreign wives. The proposal may well come from inside an affected family.
10.question: What makes Shecaniah's sentence hold guilt and hope together without canceling either?

10.title: Be Strong and Take Action
10.context: Jehohanan's chamber was a room in the temple complex used by officials. Ezra's fast here is private mourning, unlike the public fast proclaimed at the Ahava.
10.question: When someone hands you a responsibility and promises support, what does taking it up actually require first?

10.title: Trembling in the Rain
10.context: The ninth month falls in the early winter rains. The assembly stood outdoors in the square before the temple, and the weather is part of the record, not background color.
10.question: What does it say about this assembly that it answered 'we must do as you say' while standing in the rain?

10.title: Not the Work of One or Two Days
10.context: The two dissenters are named and their opposition recorded without comment. The investigation ran from the tenth month to the first, about three months of case-by-case hearings.
10.question: How do you keep a painful process both thorough and humane when it cannot be quick?

10.title: The List at the End
10.context: The book closes without narrating the outcomes household by household, and ancient readers received the ending as we do: a record, not a resolution scene. Nehemiah's book takes up the returned community a few years later.
10.question: What do you do with a story that ends on a record instead of a resolution?
